finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Only two of the four classes can be built. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), each for ONE sensor with no diagnosis: economy 2016 Hyundai Elantra 2.0L about $150-$218 (0.9-1.0 hr); midsize 2017 Hyundai Tucson 2.0L about $162-$250 (1.0-1.2 hr). Truck and luxury have parts prices but null hours, so no total is built for them. How solid the labor times are: the four Hyundai range ends are manufacturer warranty times printed with a unit (TSB 26-01-033H) and read on the government's bulletin archive; the two low ends are for the example vehicle and the two high ends are the same bulletin's times for a related vehicle. A warranty time is the low end of what a shop bills. Truck: the only maker time for a full-size pickup is GM bulletin 02-06-04-023A (June 2002), 1.5 hrs for the rear sensor on a 1999-2002 Silverado with a 0.2 hr add for three-piece engine covers. It was read on two forum-hosted PDF copies and one owners-site text copy, which all agree, but never on a government or GM page, and the 1.7 figure is an add-on sum, so both are cross-checks and the hours are left null. If the forum copies are right, the truck would come to about $246-$406 for one sensor at 1.5-1.7 hr; that is an illustration, not a built range. The government archive holds few bulletins from before about 2012, which is the likely reason this 2002 document is not there. A further search of that archive on 2026-11-20 across GM, Ford, Ram, Toyota and Nissan truck bulletins that mention the knock sensor found none that prints a replacement time with a unit: the GM, Ford and Nissan documents that loaded cover wiring repairs, software or engine replacement, and one GM special coverage bulletin for the medium-duty Kodiak and TopKick 8.1L prints 'Knock Sensor Replacement 1.0' with no unit. Luxury: no luxury-make car or crossover has a usable maker time. Genesis, Acura, Lexus, Infiniti, Lincoln, Cadillac car and crossover, Land Rover, Volkswagen group and Maserati documents that loaded either do not replace the sensor, print no time, send the dealer to the published labor time, or use time units with no conversion loaded; a Jaguar S-TYPE V6 bulletin gives 2.4 hrs for a sensor plus a sealing patch, read on a third-party site. The Cadillac Escalade entry is kept for its parts prices only, because it shares the truck's sensor and bulletin. The one maker time with a unit found for a sensor under the intake manifold on a primary page is Hyundai's 1.7 M/H for the Elantra N, which also covers an inspection and a wiring repair; it suggests the under-manifold job runs well above the 0.9-1.2 hr of the two built classes, and a Lexus, Acura, BMW or other V6 or V8 with buried sensors can take much longer still. Against the benchmarks (RepairPal $417-$589, Instant Car Fix $250-$550, J.D. Power $200-$800, FIXD $100-$400) the two built classes sit low, for three reasons: warranty times are short (RepairPal carries $291-$427 in labor, about 1.8-3.6 hours at this rate), diagnosis is not in our totals and is almost always charged for this repair, and our low parts figures are genuine sensors at online discount prices ($42) where RepairPal's parts run $126-$161. Parts: the GM sensor price is per piece; GM's own parts page sells 12589867 as a 'Pack of 1' at $133.82, the same list price the catalog sellers show next to a required quantity of 2 (two genuine sensors are about $131 online to $267.64 at list). Every low end is still a genuine sensor at an online discount. One aftermarket sensor was found on a page that states new, a Walker 242-1039 at $42.37 listed for the Silverado 1500 4.8L and 5.3L, but the page shows no model years, so it is a cross-check and not the truck low; other aftermarket sensors were listed at $27-$61 on pages that do not state condition.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (a knock sensor code can come from wiring, a connector or an engine fault, so the sensor is usually tested first), shop supplies and sales tax. Where the sensors sit under the intake manifold, expect intake manifold gaskets, the second sensor and the sensor wiring harness to be quoted at the same time, and sometimes coolant if the manifold carries it. An engine computer software update or a wiring repair is a separate charge when that is the real cause.
held_reason: Held at review after one attempt: the luxury class is a GMC Yukon Denali sharing the truck sensor and bulletin, the parts page does not confirm Denali fitment in the rows that loaded and lists a required quantity of 2, and the GM time was read on an owners-site copy of the bulletin. Hyundai times (0.9, 1.0, 1.2 M/H) and both parts prices re-read and matched. Needs a luxury-make example with a maker time. Second attempt (2026-11-20): luxury example changed to the 2002 Cadillac Escalade, which GM bulletin 02-06-04-023A names; the bulletin was read on two forum-hosted PDF copies and one owners-site text copy, still not on a government or GM page; per-piece price confirmed on GM's own parts page ('Pack of 1', $133.82). Luxury and truck share one bulletin and one sensor. Third attempt (2026-11-20): still held. About 45 bulletins on the government archive were loaded (GM, Ford and Lincoln, Honda and Acura, Hyundai and Genesis, Kia, Nissan, Toyota and Lexus, Jaguar Land Rover, Volkswagen, Subaru, Mitsubishi, Maserati); none prints a knock sensor replacement time with a unit for a full-size pickup, a truck-based SUV or a luxury-make vehicle, and GM bulletin 02-06-04-023A was not found on a government or GM page. Under the review rules the forum-copy times and the add-on sum are now labelled cross-checks and truck and luxury hours are null; the Escalade is kept for parts only. Economy and midsize unchanged. To lift: a maker time with a unit on a primary page for the truck, and an independent luxury-make example with a maker time, a genuine list price and an aftermarket new price.
